questions.stem: The temperature of a current-carrying resistor rises because:

options.explanation: Protons stay fixed in the lattice; only electrons drift.

options.text: moving electrons collide inside the wire
options.explanation: The drifting free electrons transfer energy in collisions, raising the temperature.
Charge is never generated; it only flows.
The electrical transfer warms, not cools.

questions.stem: Energy delivered to a resistor ends up:

options.explanation: The resistor does not store charge.
Only some components glow; the general outcome is heat.
Energy is conserved, never destroyed.

options.text: partly dissipated to the surroundings as heat
options.explanation: Some of the transferred energy escapes to the surroundings by heating.

questions.stem: Which appliance is deliberately built around the heating effect?

options.explanation: Toasters, kettles, heaters, ovens and hobs all exploit the heating effect.
An LED is built to avoid heating.
A clock is an electronic, not a heating, device.
A radio is an electronic device.
Current is a flow, not a store.
Current is a flow of charge, not a force.

options.text: the rate of flow of charge
options.explanation: That is the definition the note relies on.
Energy is measured in joules, current in amperes.

questions.stem: A hob heating element warms a pan mainly by:

options.explanation: The pan does not rub the element.

options.text: electrical transfer of energy in the element
options.explanation: The current in the resistive element transfers energy that then heats the pan.
No light is involved.
Static is unrelated to the mains element.

questions.stem: Name three domestic appliances that use the heating effect.
questions.modelAnswer: Electric heaters, ovens, hobs, toasters and kettles — any three of these.

questions.stem: Why does a resistor's temperature rise when current flows?
questions.modelAnswer: The free electrons drift through the lattice and collide, transferring energy to the wire, which warms up and dissipates some heat to the surroundings.

questions.stem: Explain why the heating effect counts as useful in a kettle but wasteful in long cables.
questions.modelAnswer: In a kettle the warmed element is the entire point of the device, while in a cable the heat only dissipates into the room, wasting energy and risking the insulation.

questions.stem: An electric hob warms a pan. Trace the energy pathway from the mains to the pan.
questions.modelAnswer: Mains current flows through the resistive element; the electrical transfer raises the element's temperature; the hot element then heats the pan by contact.
